To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) macroinvertebrate richness of tolerant taxa was the most responsive to human disturbance, (2) the most responsive taxa were tolerant to organic pollution, (3) models that included a variable related urbanization, runoff, and(or) riparian disturbance explained the most variance in the macroinvertabrate data, and (4) the Full Region model explained nearly as much variability in the data as Individual Eregion models, and the range in natural conditions did not appear to influence model

the Full Region model performed as well as the Individual Ecoregions models for the four macroinverbrate metrics, and that the Full Region models included variables that are relevant to human landscape modification, hydrologic disturbance, and natural disturbance.

1) the Full Region model explained 60% of the variance in the macrobenthic community data and the Individual Ecoregions models explained between 61% and 66% of the variance, 2) the Full Region and Individual Ecoregional models were equally good at explaining variance in the macrobiota data, 3) taking into account watershed area or elevation did not improve model performance, 4) models for the North Central Appalachians were the least robust
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a regional model to predict the response of macroinvertebrate communities in streams to human disturbance.

the development of predictive models to estimate the relative abundance of stream macroinvertebrate species and the relative abundance of functional feeding groups (FFGs) as a function of environmental variables.
the development of a predictive model of human landscape modification that can be used to assess the effects of human land use on stream macroinvertebrates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the best approach for developing disturbance models is still an open question, and the best answer may vary by region, metric, and other factors.
the spatial scale of the disturbance gradient is important to consider, and that the scale of the disturbance models should be matched as closely as possible to the scale of the assessment.
the Full Region models performed as well as the individual ecoregion models for predicting macroinvertebrate response.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of a regional model to evaluate human landscape modification in streams is a reasonable approach for the Northeastern United States, but that the use of individual ecoregion models is preferred when the natural landscape varies widely among ecoregion.

the best predictive models of stream macroinvertebrate response to human disturbance are developed using a regional data set, with the inclusion of a measure of human urbanization, hydrologic runoff, and natural landscape variables.

a regional disturbance model can provide a good initial assessment of overall disturbance, but the regional model should be supplemented with additional local models for specific regions and/or specific metrics to account for the effects of local natural landscape variability.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important to develop disturbance models that are specific to the region being assessed, and that the models should be based on the most relevant and available data.
the use of a single model for the full region is a viable alternative to developing multiple models for individual ecoregion.
the use of spatially broad models for assessing human landscape modifications is feasible, but it may not be possible to develop models that are robust to all spatial scales.
